articles.title: What we know about the Cornell University frat house rape investigation
articles.summary: The woman alleges she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house at the university two years ago.
articles.body:
New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024.

The woman filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house at the university.

She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved.

The men have been dubbed the "Cornell Seven" and the woman was identified as Jane Doe in court filings.

Cornell has said it supported presenting the case to a grand jury, while rejecting as "false" claims that it failed to punish those involved.

In a 101-page civil lawsuit, the woman alleged that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter allegedly assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine.

She was a 20-year-old Cornell undergraduate at the time.

Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and incapable of providing consent.

She says she left her sorority sisters after drinking that night and "stumbled alone" to the Chi Phi fraternity house in the city of Ithaca to see a male friend.

The lawsuit alleges sexual assault and battery, negligence, breach of contract and violations of New York's Human Rights Law.

It was filed against the university, fraternity sorority and men involved in the alleged attack.

The lawsuit contains an image purported to be from a fraternity group chat in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Jane Doe.

Her lawyer has said she was "traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened" in the days after the assault, which she reported to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024.

The outrage in recent weeks grew when Jane Doe alleged in her lawsuit that the men were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays".

Doe's lawyer has said two of those involved were expelled.

The university newspaper's editorial board published the names of the defendants in the lawsuit on 21 September in a piece titled "Cornell Won't, We Will", fuelling a social media outcry.

What was in the fraternity Snapchat and text messages?

The Cornell University Police Department provided an image of the Snapchat group, titled Chi Phi Actives, to prosecutors as evidence in November 2024, the university said.

The members are named in the chat and discuss a "free" sexual encounter with Jane Doe, using coarse language, just before 02:00 local time on 20 October 2024.

CBS News New York has also published excerpts of additional text messages reportedly exchanged between one of the defendants and a woman who appears to be the person who made the allegations.

The messages were reportedly sent two days after the alleged assault.

In one of the messages, one of the men appeared to apologise for "how things went down".

He said his memory was "kinda fuzzy", and that he and another man felt bad for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand".

The woman in the text chain replied saying her memory was "super clouded too" and that they were all intoxicated.

She also wrote that "non(e) of the sexual stuff was illegal", that she liked being with him and another man.

Doe suggested they smoke together again, but leave out "the extra 5 billion men and ketamine".

The woman said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police two weeks after it took place.

Shortly after, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house".

It said that the campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students".

Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law, which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities.

Following the new lawsuit, the university disputed Jane Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators.

The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell".

Cornell did not deny that the punishment for some of those involved included writing an essay.

But it said: "None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."

In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell said "temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures" were issued when the conduct was reported.

It also said the events that took place on its campus in 2024 "were appalling then and remain so now".

"We are doing all we can to foster a culture where sexual misconduct is never tolerated," it said.

The Xi Chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University

The county's top prosecutor said on Monday that his office would reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape.

Once appropriate charges were determined, the case would be prosecuted "in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, said Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.

In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges.

The prosecutor said that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from the woman's statement to authorities did not meet the legal bar to bring charges.

He said he contacted Jane Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury.

In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack, noting it differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit.

"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday.

"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

However, CBS News New York reports that it has obtained a transcript of Doe's interviews with campus police that began on 14 November - more than three weeks after the incident.

She tells police of the initial sexual encounter: "I was pretty OK with all of this."

But the outlet reports that she said of what happened later: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

articles.body: AHMEDABAD: The Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) and Indian Coast Guard seized around 526 kg of heroin and methamphetamine, valued at more than Rs 3,000 crore in the international market, after intercepting an Iranian dhow in the Arabian Sea west of Lakshadweep, officials said.The operation followed intelligence received by Gujarat ATS Police Inspector J M Patel on September 10 about a suspected international narcotics deal involving a Nigerian national and associates.The intelligence indicated that an Iranian boat named Azad was being used to transport around 500 kg of methamphetamine and heroin to Indian waters, where the consignment was to be transferred to a Tamil Nadu-based boat.According to the ATS, an advance payment for the consignment had already been made through the hawala channel, while the remaining amount was to be paid after delivery.The drugs were allegedly to be unloaded along the Tamil Nadu coast and moved in smaller quantities through different vehicles before being delivered to a Nigerian national in Punjab.Following the intelligence input, senior Gujarat ATS officers alerted the Indian Coast Guard headquarters in Delhi. Under the guidance of ATS SP K Siddharth, a team comprising inspectors B H Korot and V N Vaghela was sent to Kochi, where it joined Coast Guard officers to form a joint operation team.The team subsequently sailed aboard a Coast Guard vessel and conducted surveillance and checks of suspicious boats in the maritime area.On Friday, the vessel identified through the intelligence input was located in Indian territorial waters west of Lakshadweep.The Coast Guard intercepted and stopped the dhow, following which ATS and Coast Guard personnel boarded and searched it. The vessel was subsequently brought to Mumbai on Wednesday morning.Five Pakistani nationals were found aboard the Iranian dhow — Mohammad Yakub Balochi, Shakirullah, Faridullah, Ahmed Khan and Wahidullah Khan, all residents of Peshawar, Pakistan.A search of the vessel led to the recovery of approximately 400 kg of methamphetamine and 126 kg of heroin. articles.title: Student said encounter at frat house 'felt like coercion' in 2024 statement to police
articles.summary: ABC News obtained the woman's 2024 statement to campus police.
articles.body:
In a six-page statement given to police in November 2024, a Cornell University student told a campus police officer what happened to her at the Chi Phi fraternity house a month prior "felt like coercion," according to a copy of the police report obtained by ABC News.

The statement from the student, sworn on Nov. 15, 2024, is the most detailed account yet of what "Jane Doe" described in a civil lawsuit two years later as a "gang rape."

The former student did not call it that in her statement at the time. She did detail multiple instances where she declined to participate in certain sexual acts suggested by the men, according to the statement.

The woman's statement was central to a decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten not to bring charges in 2024.

In an interview with ABC News this week, Van Houten described the allegations as "morally disturbing" but argued Jane Doe's 2024 account of the incident suggested that she consented to the sexual activity. He said that she did not withdraw her consent, and that when she raised concerns, the fraternity members "stopped and did not pursue what they were doing."

According to her 2024 statement, at one point she said "no to the foursome" one of the fraternity brothers proposed, she said in her statement. At another point she recalled "a group of multiple men" walking into a room and "I was instantly horrified, and I remember squealing out loud and running across the room and hiding under the covers on another bed," the statement said. "I was horrified because I was really embarrassed that these individuals had seen me completely naked."

The only time Jane Doe's statement used the word "rape" came when she explained why she took an additional hit of ketamine.

"I had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out so my thought was, if I do Ketamine again maybe I will pass out. My thought was that if I passed out and these men had sex with me, then they could be charged with Rape," the statement said.

The men persisted, according to her statement.

During the final threesome, Jane Doe said, "I remember being totally disgusted at the situation, and I felt very tired and intoxicated. I would say that my level of overall intoxication was about a 8 out of 10 level of intoxicated. I would say that it was the most intoxicated I've ever been in my life. I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was," the statement said.

"To me, that felt like coercion," she wrote in the statement. "Also I felt like due to my intoxication, they should have known how intoxicated I was based on how I was slurring my words."

She recalled being so "extremely tired" she simply uttered, "Sure" when a group of men asked to snort ketamine off of her body, according to her statement. "[The] group of men all started pouring various things all over my body. I couldn't tell what they were pouring on me, as I had my face covered with my hands."

Jane Doe said she slept until 10 a.m. and was driven home by the same Chi Phi member who had originally invited her to the house and who she said had participated in the sexual acts.

By the time she woke up that Sunday afternoon, "I was made aware that what had happened to me at Chi Phi was becoming public knowledge," she wrote in the statement. "It was made clear to me by several friends that the members of Chi Phi were bragging about having an 'eightsome' with me. Some rumors said it was ten people, but nonetheless, it was now obvious that everyone knew it was me that this had happened to."

In the civil lawsuit, filed earlier this month, the woman alleged that she was drugged, assaulted and gang raped by seven former and current members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell. The lawsuit has drawn outrage and calls for an outside investigation into the matter.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has reopened the case, but has also said the allegations contained in the civil lawsuit are "dramatically different" than the woman's statement to police two years ago.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Tuesday called for an outside investigation into Cornell University's campus culture and its response to allegations by the student.

Cornell's Chi Phi chapter was barred from campus after the alleged Oct. 19, 2024, incident, though none of the individuals allegedly involved faced criminal charges, according to the DA.

Cornell University has said the former student's allegations were investigated by the university's Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards under the school's Title IX policies.

On its website, the university said the investigation was conducted over several months and included hearings before a panel of trained faculty and staff.

"At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell," the university said on its website.

Cornell said it took the reports "very seriously" and conducted a thorough investigation but said: "At the same time, responding to an incident of this seriousness cannot end when an investigation is completed or sanctions are imposed. We have an obligation to ask what more we can learn, what we can do better, and how we can reduce the likelihood that anything like this happens again."

Attorneys for multiple fraternity brothers named as defendants in the civil lawsuit have denied the allegations in the complaint.

articles.title: In 2019, staff ignored an evacuation order at Australia’s Mogo Wildlife Park, moving vulnerable animals into homes and safe areas; not one animal was lost
articles.summary: The staff at Mogo Wildlife Park stayed behind to protect roughly 200 animals as the Clyde Mountain fire approached on New Year’s Eve 2019.
articles.body: The staff at Mogo Wildlife Park stayed behind to protect roughly 200 animals as the Clyde Mountain fire approached on New Year’s Eve 2019. Smaller animals such as red pandas and monkeys were moved into homes, while lions, tigers, gorillas and orangutans were kept in protected night dens. The park later reported that every animal survived, according to ABC News. The fire reached the Mogo area on December 31 due to extreme conditions that spread across Australia's New South Wales South Coast. An evacuation order was issued for the town at about 6 a.m., but zoo director Chad Staples and his staff decided to activate the park’s fire-defence plan instead of leaving the animals behind.Staples took several red pandas and small monkeys to his own home, where they could be sheltered indoors, and a later report said approximately 25 animals were moved into his house, including pandas and monkeys. The larger animals such as giraffes and zebras were given access to paddocks where staff had reduced the fire risk, while dangerous species such as lions, tigers, gorillas and orangutans were encouraged into their night dens. Staff also used large quantities of water to wet grass and structures that could burn. ABC reported that staff moved vehicles that carried water and pumps around the grounds and attacked smaller fires as they appeared.The zoo had prepared for a fireStaff had already developed a fire-defence plan for the 81-acre wildlife park, and the plan dictated where different animals should go if a bushfire approached. Mogo itself was badly damaged, with businesses and homes destroyed as the fire moved through the area. Staff at the wildlife park therefore had to operate inside a disaster that was affecting the town around them.Staples told ABC that the keepers moved lions, tigers and other dangerous animals into their night dens and tried to maintain normal routines, while larger herbivores were given more freedom within protected areas rather than being forced into unfamiliar transport. The strategy also meant that staff could respond to changing conditions, as spot fires could be attacked quickly, water could be moved where it was needed and animals could remain in familiar surroundings instead of being transported during the worst part of the fire. Mogo Wildlife Park reopened to visitors in February 2020, about two months after the fire, and ABC reported that the park had suffered damage to its perimeter fence but was otherwise largely unscathed and that all of its animals had been kept safe.The animals returned as the park recoveredStaff had to repair parts of the property while also taking care of the animals. The zoo also became involved in the wider aftermath of the bushfires, and there were plans for veterinary support for native wildlife that were injured in the surrounding fires. Some animals had spent the worst hours in buildings or dens, while others remained outside in protected paddocks. The smallest animals were physically removed from the most vulnerable parts of the park and sheltered at staff members’ homes.Mogo Wildlife Park remains open today and operates under Australian Wildlife Parks. Its current collection includes giraffes, zebras, gorillas, rhinoceroses, tigers, red pandas, primates and other species, and the park’s own history describes its survival during the Black Summer bushfires as a defining part of its story.Then-NSW Rural Fire Service Commissioner Shane Fitzsimmons described Mogo as an example of planning for bushfires and other disasters at its 2020 reopening, and pointed specifically to the fact that the animals survived despite the damage around the property.The impressive fact is that the fire plan had been built around the animals that were already at the park, and when the evacuation order came, staff knew which animals could be moved, which needed shelter and which were safer remaining in familiar paddocks. That system was put into use as flames and smoke reached Mogo, and the park emerged with its animal collection intact.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Irish public sector: More than 100,000 workers take industrial action
articles.summary: Two days of fuller strike action have been planned for 14 and 21 October, when it is expected schools will be closed and picket lines formed across the country.
articles.body:
Some health, education and council workers in the Republic of Ireland have commenced industrial action over an ongoing public sector pay dispute.

More than 100,000 workers, including nurses, school staff and civil servants, moved to work-to-rule measures on Wednesday morning.

The Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) said its public health service staff will perform only duties necessary for safe patient care and "will not work any additional unpaid hours".

Two days of fuller strike action have been planned for 14 and 21 October, when it is expected schools could be closed and picket lines formed across the country.

INMO said nurses and midwives who have taken work-to-rule action "will not attend non-clinical meetings, except where attendance is strictly necessary for direct patient care".

They have been joined by Fórsa, the Republic's largest public sector union, after 96.6% of their members who voted in an industrial ballot did so in favour of action.

Members of SIPTU, who represent public sector workers in health and administration, have also signed up to work-to-rule measures.

On their website Fórsa said "there are currently no talks taking place" with the Irish government in relation to a new public sector pay deal, after the previous arrangement expired on 30 June.

They said dialogue with state employers has been held up by the "government's unwillingness to address cost-of-living measures at the start of any negotiations".

They added: "With no public service agreement in place, we are now in dispute with government, as the employer of public service workers."

SIPTU Divisional Organiser Brendan O'Brien said the "goodwill" of workers was a large part of what kept public services going, but said the Irish government's failure to establish a basis for formal talks "left our members with no alternative but to act collectively".

He added: "We are calling on public service employers and the government to engage constructively and urgently to avoid an escalation of this dispute."

Ireland's Department of Public Expenditure told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that unions and representative associations have taken industrial action rather than engaged in talks.

"It is deeply unfair on the general public for there to be significant disruption to their daily lives because unions are unwilling to sit down and engage constructively on a new agreement," a spokesperson said.

"Officials remain ready and willing to engage and that should happen without any further delay."

"Meaningful progress can only be achieved where both parties are open to constructive and sustained engagement, without preconditions on either side," the Department added.

The teaching unions Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland (ASTI) and Irish National Teachers' Organisation (INTO) have confirmed they will begin work-to-rule action on 5 October, before moving to a full one-day strike on 14 October.

ASTI said up to 20,000 secondary school teachers will take part.

INTO, which represents a a majority of primary school teachers, said it intended on a second one-day strike on 21 October.

Rank-and-file members of the Garda Representative Association have also announced several days of action calling for better conditions.

articles.title: In 2024, a Houston Zoo ride-out team stayed overnight during Hurricane Beryl; all enclosures remained secure and the animals were cared for throughout the outage
articles.summary: During Hurricane Beryl in July 2024, the Houston Zoo's dedicated ride-out team stayed overnight to ensure the safety and well-being of the animals. Despite power outages and storm damage, all animal enclosures remained secure, showcasing the zoo's emergency preparedness and commitment to animal care.
articles.body: Hurricane Beryl struck Texas in July 2024 and knocked out power at the Houston Zoo, but a ride-out team stayed overnight to watch over the animals and the zoo’s critical systems. The storm damaged multiple parts of the property, and Houston had to deal with widespread outages, yet the zoo reported that its animal enclosures remained secure and the animals continued receiving care throughout the outage.Hurricane Beryl made landfall near Matagorda, Texas, on July 8, 2024, as a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 80 mph. The National Weather Service reported widespread wind damage across Southeast Texas, including an 89-mph wind gust that was recorded at the University of Houston and an 84-mph gust at William P. Hobby Airport. The storm also brought heavy rain and widespread power outages across the Houston area, according to National Weather Service records.For the zoo, losing electricity meant more than turning off lights, since animal-care facilities depend on power for equipment, temperature control and other systems, while staff also have to keep food, water and medical care available during an extended disruption. The ride-out team stayed on the grounds through the storm rather than leaving the animals unattended. The group included staff responsible for animal care, veterinary services, facilities and other essential operations, with their job being to monitor the animals, check enclosures and respond if the storm created a problem inside the zoo.The animals stayed in protected areasAnimals were moved into protected spaces such as barns and night houses as the storm approached, which reduced their exposure to wind and rain while allowing keepers to continue their normal care routines. The Houston Zoo said that its staff had prepared for the storm before Beryl arrived, and generators were available to support essential operations during the power outage, while employees monitored buildings, animal areas and equipment throughout the night.The zoo is home to thousands of animals representing hundreds of species, so the response could not be reduced to a single evacuation decision. Different species have different housing requirements, and having to move large or unfamiliar animals during a storm can create additional risks. Staff therefore focused on keeping the animals in secure areas and maintaining the systems that they depended on. The zoo's storm preparations also included checking trees and other potential hazards around enclosures, in order to secure objects that could become debris and ensuring that emergency equipment was available. The National Weather Service recorded the storm's progression across the Houston region as Beryl moved inland, where it was seen that wind damage brought down trees and power lines in multiple communities, which contributed to the prolonged outages that followed the hurricane's passage.Power was out, but animal care continuedZoo staff had to rely on backup systems without the normal electrical supply, while crews inspected the property. Staff checked the enclosures and made sure the animals had food and water, and the zoo also worked to clear storm debris and assess damage around the grounds. The zoo reported fallen trees and damage to some buildings and infrastructure, but none of the animal enclosures were breached.A damaged enclosure can turn a storm-related power failure into an animal emergency, and keeping the barriers intact meant keepers could continue working with the animals in their usual secure spaces instead of attempting emergency relocations. KPRC reported that staff were dealing with fallen trees, flooding and damage to parts of the campus while continuing to care for the animals. The report also explained how zoo staff prepare animals and their habitats for major storms.The zoo reopened after the stormBeryl moved away from Houston, but the zoo's response continued after the winds and rain stopped, which included having to remove fallen branches and dealing with areas affected by flooding before visitors could return. The Houston Zoo remained closed during the initial cleanup period, and staff continued working on the property while maintaining the animals' daily routines.The storm produced hurricane-force winds, widespread tree and power-line damage and major disruptions across the Houston area before weakening as it moved farther inland, but for the zoo's animals, the immediate emergency ended without an enclosure breach. The ride-out team had remained on site through the storm and keepers continued feeding and monitoring the animals while the campus was without normal power. The damage to the grounds took longer to address, but the animal-care operation continued throughout the disruption.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2020, five workers remained at a South Australian wildlife park as bushfires approached, choosing to defend the 700 animals in their care
articles.summary: In January 2020, five dedicated workers at the Kangaroo Island Wildlife Park brave catastrophic bushfires to protect 700 animals, showcasing an extraordinary commitment to wildlife care amid disaster.
articles.body: In January 2020, as catastrophic bushfires swept across Kangaroo Island in South Australia, the Kangaroo Island Wildlife Park faced a difficult decision. Evacuation warnings were in place around Parndana as flames approached the property, but moving hundreds of animals was not a practical option. According to The Guardian, park owner Sam Mitchell and four other close friends and family members remained behind to defend the park and the roughly 800 animals in their care. The group worked alongside Country Fire Service personnel as the fire threatened the property. The park was already caring for wildlife affected by the fires, including koalas, when the danger reached its doorstep. What followed was a long effort to protect the animals, buildings and enclosures while fire moved through the surrounding landscape.Staying as the fire approachedThis decision was made in very dangerous conditions as the fire approached. By 9 January, there were warnings from the authorities that all residents near Parndana should evacuate, but the fire was still spreading over the island. The park was located west of Parndana, and many injured animals due to the previous fires sought shelter there. Those who stayed could not simply load all the animals into cars and leave, because the park housed species with different care, feeding and handling needs.The Country Fire Service offered assistance, while park staff and their families managed the threat from spot fires. At one point, flames came within 100 meters of the park, and the team worked for about 48 hours to keep them away from the animals and buildings. It was not only the animals in the park that were at risk. Kangaroo Island was one of the worst affected regions in the Black Summer bushfires, and the park also became part of the effort to care for injured wildlife.A refuge during a wider wildlife disasterThe scale of the disaster helps explain how the park's role changed during the fires. Kangaroo Island's bushfires had burned a large portion of the island and damaged important habitat for species found nowhere else. Research published in Animals examined 304 records of koalas rescued after the 2019-20 Kangaroo Island fires. The study found that 67.4% of the koalas recorded had burns, while 77.1% were dehydrated and 74.6% of burnt animals were in poor body condition. The findings showed that treating surviving wildlife involved more than dealing with visible burns, as dehydration, poor nutrition, and the severity of injuries also affected outcomes.The wildlife park became part of that broader response. After the immediate threat passed, animal-care organisations including RSPCA South Australia sent veterinary and animal-handling teams to the park. On 10 January, the RSPCA reported that its staff were helping care for wildlife at the facility, particularly koalas suffering burns and malnutrition after losing much of their natural food supply. This meant the park was serving two purposes at once: protecting its permanent collection while providing a place where injured native animals could receive care.What the fires changed for wildlife careThe event also prompted a wider review of how prepared wildlife organisations were for disasters like this. The 2019-20 bushfires affected wildlife across several Australian states. Zoos, wildlife hospitals, government departments and conservation groups had to work together to rescue and treat animals and plan for their long-term recovery. The Kangaroo Island Wildlife Park’s experience showed how urgent this issue was for wildlife organisations. Evacuating people from a fast-moving fire is difficult enough; relocating a large number of captive animals is just as challenging.The park escaped the immediate danger of the fire, even though the surrounding island had already suffered considerable ecological damage. The focus moved on to attending to animals whose lives had been disrupted by the incident. In that sense, the story is less about one night of defending a wildlife park and more about how natural disasters affect animal-care facilities. For the five people who stayed, the task in January 2020 was clear: protect the animals that could not care for themselves.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Taiwan analysts say Trump-Xi summit produced no policy shift but real test lies ahead
articles.summary: Taiwan analysts assess whether Xi Jinping secured private concessions from Trump, with arms sales and senior U.S. official visits as key tests ahead.
articles.body: TAIPEI — Taiwanese officials were watching carefully for signs of policy changes toward the island as President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit last week in Washington, D.C. Xi’s visit was of high interest in Taiwan, a regular target of China’s threats. On Saturday, a panel that included scholars, a retired U.S. military officer and Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister at the Institute for National Policy Research (INPR) in Taipei assessed what the third Trump–Xi meeting of Trump’s current term means for Taiwan. Most expect no change in U.S. policy toward Taiwan. "Both of them got what they want and what they need," Kuo Yu-jen, INPR’s vice president and a professor at National Sun Yat-sen University’s Institute of China and Asia-Pacific Studies, told Fox News Digital. Trump can point to economic results from negotiating with Xi, while Xi can return to Beijing with the prestige of a high-profile U.S. reception, Kuo said. He called claims by some that Trump had "sold out" Taiwan excessive speculation. XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE' As expected, Xi reportedly pressed Trump to say the United States opposes Taiwan independence. Washington’s preferred description is that it does not support Taiwan independence, a distinction that, much to the relief of Taiwan government officials, Trump maintained. Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital after the forum, Taiwan’s Deputy Foreign Minister François Wu said Beijing wants more than a change in diplomatic language. It wants the world to view Taiwan as a domestic Chinese issue. If that argument succeeds, Wu said, Beijing could claim other countries have no right to respond to its actions against the island. "The so-called independence of Taiwan is just an issue made specifically by the Chinese government," Wu said. Taiwan already has a president and government elected by its people, territory and its own currency, he said. "We just don’t need to declare any independence. We are a sovereign country." Wu had expressed concerns prior to Trump’s visit to China in May, when he told Bloomberg that "What we are most afraid of is to put Taiwan on the menu of the talk between Xi Jinping and President Trump." China’s Foreign Ministry claims Xi urged Trump to maintain the "correct position" to oppose Taiwan independence. Taiwan’s Foreign Ministry rushed out an objection on a public holiday in Taiwan, and repeated Taiwan’s own clear position on its sovereignty. CHINA DEPLOYED OVER 100 VESSELS NEAR TAIWAN IN THE WAKE OF TRUMP-XI SUMMIT, TAIWAN SECURITY OFFICIAL CLAIMS The White House summary of Xi’s visit announced no change in Taiwan policy and instead emphasized more favorable tariff treatment for $30 billion in goods in each direction, an AI incident communication channel and U.S. concerns about rare earth and critical-mineral supplies. The visit nonetheless raised questions in Taiwan about what Xi might have obtained from Trump in private. Analysts cautioned that if there was a deal over Taiwan, it would only become clear in the coming months. Taiwan awaits Trump’s approval for more arms sales, visits to Taiwan by senior U.S. officials and a potential transit stop in the U.S. for Taiwan’s president. China objects to all of these, so how Trump handles them must balance relations with China, maintaining support for Taiwan and Trump’s priorities. Dong Li-wen, executive director of the government-funded Foundation on Asia-Pacific Peace Studies, described the leaders’ shared approach as delaying difficult decisions while waiting for circumstances to change. For Xi, Dong argued, that is a longer-term strategy. For Trump, it is a temporary tactic. The two sides can keep talking and set aside issues they cannot settle, but their underlying competition remains. The argument over Taiwan’s status is almost 80 years old. China claims the island as its territory, but the People’s Republic of China has not governed it for even a single day. The Republic of China government relocated to Taiwan after the Chinese Nationalists lost the civil war to Mao Zedong’s Communists in 1949. The governing Democratic Progressive Party’s 1999 Resolution on Taiwan’s Future described Taiwan as an independent sovereign state called the Republic of China under its existing constitution. All of Taiwan’s democratically elected presidents have said something similar in interviews with international media, including Lee Teng-hui to The Washington Post in 1997, Chen Shui-bian to the BBC in 2010, Ma Ying-jeou to CNN in 2010, and Tsai Ing-wen to the BBC in 2020. Current President William Lai Ching-te said the same thing to Time in 2024, adding an oft-repeated insistence that the Republic of China and the People’s Republic of China are not subordinate to each other. That status quo — which amounts to Taiwan being a de facto independent state — is what Taiwan intends to defend, according to Deputy Foreign Minister Wu. Xi left Washington having restated China’s demands. Analysts at the gathering said whether Xi managed to nudge U.S. policy in any way will soon be tested in decisions over arms sales and other issues, with some predicting weapons packages could be scaled down or "unbundled." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Speaking separately to Fox News Digital, Ross Darrell Feingold, a political analyst and assistant professor at Tamkang University’s Department of Diplomacy and International Relations, noted that with a local election in Taiwan this November, followed by presidential and legislative elections in January 2028, Taiwan’s domestic politics could also be a factor in U.S. decisions. "Although the U.S. is likely to back President Lai’s re-election; agreeing to arms sales, visits by Trump administration officials or Lai’s desired transit stop in the U.S. will need to be balanced against coming across as too blatantly interfering in Taiwan’s election, as well as the inevitable anger from China."

articles.title: ‘We no longer eat three meals’: Yemen’s displaced face daily fight for food
articles.summary: Yemen’s latest fighting has redrawn front lines after more than a decade of war, deepening hunger and displacement.
articles.body:
Mohamed Saed’s children still call him to the table. “Come on, Dad, come eat,” they say. Often, he tells them he is already full, even when he has gone without food.

The 46-year-old teacher has not received a salary in years. Displaced three or four times since Yemen’s war began, he lives with his wife and five children in a single room in Taiz and is more than a year behind on rent.

“We no longer eat three meals,” he told Al Jazeera. “Maybe two meals and sometimes one meal.”

His family was going hungry long before the latest fighting. Now, a new escalation that began in early September has forced nearly 134,000 people from their homes, including an estimated 73,000 children, according to UNICEF, leaving many more families deciding which meals to skip.

Yemen’s latest round of fighting has redrawn front lines after more than a decade of war, fuelling hunger and displacement.

The country has been effectively divided since the Iran-aligned Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. The Houthis control the north and west, where most Yemenis live, while the internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, holds most of the south and east.

On September 3, fighting erupted between the Houthis and government forces when the Houthis launched a major offensive west of Taiz.

Within days, Houthi fighters entered Mocha, and they have since taken control of almost all of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, down to the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a chokepoint for global shipping.

Saudi Arabia has responded with hundreds of air strikes, and the Houthis have launched drone and missile attacks on Saudi territory.

The World Health Organization (WHO) says 838 people have been killed and more than 3,600 injured since early August, when the Houthis began striking government forces.

Most of the toll has come since the ground offensive began on September 3, and in the week to September 26 alone, 164 people were killed. UNICEF has verified that at least 15 children have been killed and 14 injured since September 3, and three more are reported missing.

Ruqqaya Saeed is 25 and a mother of eight. She fled Zaghar, in the Maqbanah area west of Taiz where the Houthi offensive began, facing what she describes as rockets, shells and the terror of landmines all at once.

“We left our homes, and we left our livestock, the donkey and the chickens”, she told Al Jazeera from al-Shaqadif camp near Taiz city. “We left everything up to God.”

In the camp, she says, no aid organisation has brought her family food. They survive on what charitable people give them. She borrowed money to buy a tarpaulin for shelter, and rainwater has already soaked through it twice, drenching their clothes.

Her children are sick. “The children have diarrhoea, colds and dysentery. We don’t have water for them, not even clean water,” she says.

Dysentery, an intestinal infection spread by contaminated water and poor sanitation, can be deadly for young children because of dehydration.

“There are no blankets to keep warm,” Saeed says. “We only give them treatment at home with water, salt and sugar.”

There are no toilets in the camp. Women wait until night and walk to the mountainside or somewhere isolated, she says.

In a country of about 43 million people, more than 18.3 million face acute food insecurity in 2026, according to the UN.

Children are among the hardest hit. Even before the latest fighting, more than 2.2 million children under five were projected to be acutely malnourished this year, more than half a million of them with severe acute malnutrition, the deadliest form, UNICEF’s Louise Wateridge told Al Jazeera.

She warned that the fighting is accelerating a vicious cycle: conflict drives hunger and hunger leaves children more vulnerable to conflict.

In government-controlled areas, nearly five million people, about half, faced crisis levels of hunger or worse between March and May, including 1.4 million in emergency conditions, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), the global standard for measuring hunger.

The IPC projected that the situation would worsen during the June to September lean season, with 5.3 million people facing crisis conditions or worse, including 1.6 million in emergency conditions.

Even after the harvest, it expects 5.4 million to remain at crisis levels or worse from October to December.

Enas Abdullah Abdo, 23, fled Hadhran with her three children on the second day of fighting.

“Every hour, the shelling and clashes on us increased, [and] then when the shells eventually reached the houses, we were forced to leave”, she says. Cars could no longer reach them, so the family set out on foot and walked until they found one.

“When we left, we didn’t take anything”, Abdo says. They left without kitchen supplies, mattresses, blankets or batteries for light.

For the past month, about 15 people from five families, her siblings with their spouses and children, have shared a small, damaged house in al-Nashama. “If it rains, the rain falls on us, on the children and on our clothes”, she says. If they cannot find more space, they may have to return to a camp.

An aid organisation gave the family 270,000 Yemeni riyals (about $170), which they spent on essentials including gas cylinders and a few blankets. They still lack food, bedding and medicine. When the children fall ill, treatment at health centres is often incomplete or costs more than they can pay.

“Sometimes we go to the health centres and we don’t find complete treatment, so we’re forced to go back home and give them regular painkillers”, she says.

The displacement has also interrupted the children’s schooling. Of the five or six children in the wider family who were in school before they fled, only three or four have been able to go back. The others could not bring their school records.

Abdo has already lost a brother to an earlier round of fighting, and both her parents to illness.

articles.title: What’s behind French student protests that turned violent?
articles.summary: The school protests coincide with public sector strikes over planned budget cuts.
articles.body:
Protests over crowded classrooms, teacher shortages and lengthy school days have spread across France, with police detaining more than 400 people, many of them minors, on Tuesday.

The movement began at high schools in the Paris area last week before expanding nationwide. Some school blockades turned violent as protesters burned rubbish bins and hurled bottles at officers, who responded with batons and tear gas. Authorities said 48 law enforcement officers were injured.

The unrest coincided with a public sector strike over the government’s budget plans, adding to political tensions and a headache for Emmanuel Macron ahead of next year’s presidential election. Here is what we know.

The French education ministry says protests have affected about 400 of France’s 3,700 lycees (high schools).

Protests began in Paris last week, where teenagers have been blockading their schools for several days. This week, demonstrations and blockades have spread around the country. On Tuesday, protesters set fire to rubbish bins outside a high school in Lille, northern France, and threw bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at police.

Confrontations have also been reported in Bordeaux, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon and Marseille. In some cases, officers responded with tear gas after bus shelters and advertising hoardings were vandalised. According to AFP, high school students piled up rubbish bins at the entrance to the Lycee Gabriel Guist’hau in Nantes.

About 80 students gathered outside the Lamartine school in Paris, brandishing slogans complaining of getting “More hours of lessons than sleep”.

At the Lycee Brequigny in the northwestern city of Rennes, Brittany’s largest high school, about 100 students threw projectiles at the building, an AFP video journalist reported.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told BFM TV that 440 people had been detained nationwide, although the tally was not final. About two-thirds were subsequently placed in police custody, he said.

Nunez condemned protesters who arrived with their faces covered and carrying projectiles, saying there was no justification for seeking confrontations with officers. He also said there had been seven incidents in which hydrochloric acid was thrown at police. AFP reported that police carrying riot shields struck students with batons when a crowd formed in the Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis.

Vincent Latour, professor of British studies at Universite Toulouse Jean Jaures, told Al Jazeera the movement was expanding. “The number of secondary schools involved has doubled over the last couple of days,” he said.

The protests are over conditions in France’s lycees, where students generally spend their final three years of secondary education, between the ages of 15 and 18.

Their complaints include large class sizes, absent teachers, inadequate school buildings and exhausting schedules. Outside the Lamartine lycee in Paris, students held placards protesting against their timetables, the UK’s Guardian newspaper reported. One read: “8am-6pm. More hours of lessons than sleep.”

Latour said the grievances had been building since heatwaves in June exposed problems with school buildings. “There has been discontent since successive heatwaves in June this year, which revealed the poor state of schools, with poor insulation and no air conditioning,” he said.

“The current wave is happening against a background of difficult conditions: missing teachers, teachers who are absent and not replaced, continued difficult material conditions, and discontent over working conditions and pay.”

In Saint-Denis, north of Paris, Mayor Bally Bagayoko joined hundreds of students outside the Paul-Eluard lycee. He described their protest as “completely legitimate” and said poorer areas received fewer resources than wealthier ones.

Latour said some students also questioned the government’s priorities, pointing to its emphasis on restrictions such as the ban on wearing the abaya in state schools.

“Some students argue they should concentrate on what matters: offering pupils and students decent learning conditions,” he said.

How are the protests linked to the strikes?

The school protests coincided with a nationwide public-sector strike against the government’s proposed budget, which includes 54 billion euros ($61.3bn) of funding cuts and savings.

Caroline Cheve, secretary-general of the FSU education union federation, said pupils and teachers essentially shared the same frustrations.

“They’re in overcrowded classrooms. Sometimes they don’t have enough teachers because of staffing shortages. They see the same reality as we do, and they’re angry,” she said.

The government also proposes freezing state employees’ base salaries in 2027 to save about 2 billion euros ($2.27bn). Unions say this would be the fourth consecutive annual freeze.

Teachers, firefighters and other public sector workers therefore joined Tuesday’s action by students. The education ministry said just over 11 percent of teachers and other school staff participated. Ryad Rani, president of the Union Syndicale Lyceenne, a high school students’ union, called for nationwide school blockades alongside the public sector strike, while urging protesters to “remain peaceful”.

He said students were protesting against a “general lack of resources”, classes containing as many as 32 to 35 pupils, and shortages of teachers and other staff.

Rani criticised instructions from the interior and education ministries telling police to maintain order outside schools with a proportionate use of force.

“We’re talking about pupils of 15-18 years old and the government’s only response is automatic and institutionalised repression. It’s unacceptable,” he told BFM TV.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu condemned violence outside schools and accused political opponents of encouraging an escalation. “Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff or police,” he wrote on X.

Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, accused the government of ordering a crackdown on high school students. “This brutality is irresponsible and has a clear racist undertone. Hands off our youth,” he wrote, calling on elected officials and party activists to intervene.

Lecornu called Melenchon’s intervention an “irresponsible escalation” and rejected the accusation of racism as “an insult”.

“Exploiting their anger for partisan purposes is wrong,” he wrote.

The dispute comes as Lecornu seeks support for the 2027 budget in a divided parliament, while parties position themselves ahead of the presidential election next spring.

Latour said the school protests were unfolding amid wider anger over public services, high fuel prices and pressure on household finances. “The political climate is rather explosive because of the upcoming presidential election,” he said.

He suggested left-wing parties could seek to bring different protest movements together, including those involving school pupils.

Latour also said unrest could spread to universities, where funding pressures had intensified. “There is potential for a series of protests in French universities, given the underfunding of French universities over the past few years,” he said.

“There was a deterioration over the last year, which seems set to continue.”

articles.title: The October 7 warnings threatening Netanyahu’s Israeli election campaign
articles.summary: Netanyahu faces continued pressure over alleged warnings before the 2023 Hamas attack as October 27 elections draw near.
articles.body:
The controversy over warnings Benjamin Netanyahu is alleged to have received in advance of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks continues to dog the Israeli prime minister ahead of knife-edge elections slated for October 27.

The latest blow to Netanyahu came on Sunday, after a Wall Street Journal report suggested that he had been warned of the attack by Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, who reportedly phoned the prime minister just days before the attack, underscoring previous warnings in September 2023, when he is said to have flown to Israel to warn security officials in person that Hamas was planning an attack.

News of Kamel’s warnings follows reports in Israeli and US media earlier this month suggesting that Netanyahu had been warned by United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ) in the week before the attack that Hamas’s then-leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, was planning the assault.

Netanyahu has been emphatic in his denials of having received any warning of an attack, and has sued over the claims.

Neither Kamel nor the Egyptian government has commented on the reports. The UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said it does not comment on media reports or speculation concerning conversations between government leaders.

Netanyahu has attempted to shift the blame for not being alerted to the attack onto the former head of Israel’s internal security service, Ronen Bar, who announced on Monday that he would sue the prime minister, a longtime political nemesis , for defamation as a result.

Polling suggests that events surrounding the October 7 attacks, which killed 1,139 people in Israel, and questions over responsibility for security failures that preceded them remain important issues for voters ahead of the upcoming parliamentary elections. Continued media coverage has also kept the trauma of the attack at the centre of public debate, more than three years after Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza, killing more than 74,000 Palestinians.

“We know that Egypt’s Chief of Intelligence flew to Israel on September 26 and warned Israel of a … Hamas attack,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said. “We also know that similar messages came from MBZ.”

“Why they were ignored? That’s the magic of what we call ‘conception’,” he said, referring to ha-conceptzia, the Hebrew term for the underlying assumptions on which Israeli security decisions are often based. “And Israel, not only Netanyahu, believed in the conception that Hamas was deterred and all it wanted was to [push] Israel a little bit to ease the pressure and blockade on Gaza.”

Netanyahu’s two main rivals in the race for prime minister have both seized on the alleged warnings.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the Beyachad (Together) alliance, said if the allegations were proven true, Netanyahu “cannot continue to serve in his position for another minute”. Former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party leads Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls by the slenderest of margins, said, “Netanyahu received dozens of warnings for October 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit.”

The reports do not appear to have had a significant effect on the election polls, but, all the same, the latest revelations in The Wall Street Journal were likely to concern those within Netanyahu’s campaign who had already invested significant time and effort in rebutting the initial round of stories claiming he had been warned by the UAE leader, London-based Israeli academic and media analyst Ayala Panievsky told Al Jazeera.

“However, the opinion polls have been quite stable for years now. I wouldn’t expect a significant portion of Netanyahu voters to break with him over this,” she said. “It could hurt him with voter turnout and excitement among his base, however, which could be significant as the polls seem relatively close.”

Analysts suggested that part of the explanation lay in the Likud party’s and Netanyahu’s longstanding portrayal of themselves as political outsiders under attack from what they were encouraged to see as a hostile political establishment. That narrative may make supporters more inclined to accept the prime minister’s denials and his criticism of the security services and other institutions.

“I think everyone expected [the reports on Netanyahu being given warnings] to be a landmark story, one serious enough to really damage Netanyahu,” Israeli political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg said.

“However, Netanyahu’s rebuttals and threats to sue have given his supporters something to hold on to,” Flaschenberg said. “They’re now free to dismiss the stories as fake, just as the opposition is pushing them. The politics of this really have become that entrenched.”

However, analysts cautioned that it remains unclear whether acting on any warnings would ultimately have prevented an attack on the scale of October 7. They also pointed to the wider context in Gaza, where years of Israeli restrictions and military actions, widely condemned by rights groups, the United Nations, and a number of states, had contributed to deep grievances and a heightened risk of violence.

“Strategic surprises cannot be prevented,” Bregman continued.

“A determined opponent will eventually inflict on you an October 7. You can delay it. Prevent it temporarily, but you can’t stop it,” he said, “Israel’s next October 7 will come from the West Bank. Not now, but in the future. Maybe in five, 10, 30 years, but it’s inevitable.”

articles.title: Danni from Dorset becomes first contestant to leave Bake Off
articles.summary: Danni from Dorset was the first of 12 contestants to leave 17th series of the Great British Bake Off.
articles.body:
An HGV service administrator from Dorset has become the first person to leave this year's Great British Bake Off.

Danni was eliminated from the Channel 4 TV series during biscuit week after being told by judge Paul Hollywood their cookies were "powdery".

During the episode, which aired on Tuesday, Danni said they had been unable to taste the cookies because the ingredients included cream and butter and they were vegan.

They said competing on Bake Off gave them "some of the best advice about how to improve something that I love".

Speaking to BBC Radio Solent's Dorset Breakfast show, they said: "It was absolutely fantastic, on and off camera. I was just hyped to be there.

"Some of my favourite parts were the technicals which I was consistently not great on doing but I loved doing them so much... It's like a puzzle."

Reflecting on their time in the tent, Danni said: "I've never been the best with making friends.

"I'm quite an eccentric person and quite a Marmite person.

"Going into it, I wasn't expecting to make friends. I wasn't expecting there to be so many lovely, lovely people.

"It wasn't a competitive environment at all, it's just a bit of fun you are having with your friends."

Hairdresser Tom, from West Yorkshire, was named star baker on Tuesday.

During the episode, bakers made American-style cookies, recreated iced gems and created a "visually striking" biscuit mosaic.

Danni explained to Hollywood and fellow judge Nigella Lawson that they were vegan so could not try their own cinnamon "Snickerdoodle" cookies, topped with peanut brittle.

Tasting the bakes, Lawson said the cookies had "too much cinnamon and bicarb", adding: "It's impossible to know what you are baking if you don't taste it."

Following their elimination, Danni said: "I am really happy that I was the first one out because I know everyone in there has more skills than me.

"But I think I've learned something about myself, which is that in the right circumstances I can make quite a few friends.

"Finding love in a group of strangers – that's just beautiful."

They added: "Of all the bakers there, I was easily the weakest, which isn't bad at all.

"It means I have 11 other people to bug about baking questions now whenever I want."

articles.title: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends
articles.summary: The withdrawal of coalition forces, under a deal agreed two years ago, was a key demand of the Iraqi government.
articles.body:
The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country.

The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday.

It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month.

British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability".

Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal.

US plans to cut off military aid to key Middle East ally, BBC told

Saudi Arabia joins US in strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq

'Attacked 28 times in a day' - BBC visits heavily targeted US-UK base in Iraq

"Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym.

"With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership."

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq".

He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq."

The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence.

A recent UN report estimated that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only".

The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country.

Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit.

But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence.

Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base.

Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose.

A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran.

They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby.

At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day.

RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.

On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission.

It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region.

It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold.

The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners.

US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan.

US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters.

This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq.

Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.

They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist.

The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel.

US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country.

articles.title: David Bowie's ban lifted at Brighton Dome for new exhibition
articles.summary: An immersive exhibition exploring the life and work of David Bowie is set to open at Brighton Dome.
articles.body:
An immersive exhibition exploring the life and work of a music icon is set to be held at Brighton Dome.

David Bowie: You're Not Alone uses film, photography and audio to showcase rarely seen material from the David Bowie Archive in New York.

David Bowie was banned from Brighton Dome for life after fans tore up seats during a 1973 concert on his Ziggy Stardust tour.

Lucy Davies, director and chief executive of Brighton Dome, told the BBC the venue had "forgiven" Bowie and "welcomed him back".

"The exhibition is an incredibly emotional, euphoric, beautiful work of art and I'm really proud and excited to bring it to Brighton," she says.

Davies said it was "an honour" to lift the ban on musician.

The immersive light and sound experience blends some of Bowie's most legendary live performances with interviews, photographs, artwork and lyrics.

Its producers were given unprecedented access to the Bowie Archive in New York working through thousands of hours of recordings to help create the exhibition.

Alan Edwards, who was Bowie's publicist for nearly four decades, was the show's consultant producer.

He told BBC Bowie had kept a lot of his personal archive.

"There's a warehouse in New York with books and everything you could think of, all his stage shows and more," he said.

"Mark Grimmer, the main organiser of the exhibition, went to the warehouse and began opening boxes and cans of film, tape and things that had never been seen before.

"He pieced together all the words, so we have a show in David's own voice, which was quite incredible."

Edwards said it was "not easy" to put together the show, describing it as a "labour of love".

The exhibition is currently at the Lightroom in London's King's Cross.

"I think what David would have loved was so many of his musical friends - David Gilmour, Noel Gallagher, Goldie, Neil Tennant - went to see [the exhibition] and they were moved by it in different ways," Edwards said.

"I felt David smiling down on us on those days and he would have approved it."

David Bowie: You're Not Alone is due to be displayed at Brighton Dome from 16 July to 30 August 2027.

articles.body: A leading American evangelical leader has condemned remarks made by a Palestinian official claiming the Bible as a "Palestinian book." Palestinian Ambassador to the U.K. Husam Zomlot made the comments earlier this month at the University of Bradford as the revisionist argument takes shape asserting Jesus was a Palestinian. Zomlot’s claims that the Bible is a "Palestinian book" and that, by extension, all Christians are Palestinian has drawn sharp criticism from those who say the remarks advance a contested historical narrative about the land. THE WAR ON AMERICA’S JUDEO-CHRISTIAN ROOTS THREATENS EVERYTHING WE SHARE "The Palestinians aren’t the ‘people of the Book.’ When the ‘Book’ was written, the term Palestinian had not yet been coined," Pastor John Hagee, founder and chairman of Christians United for Israel (CUFI), told Fox News Digital. "The Palestinian ambassador’s attempt to claim the Jewish mantle of religion and history as his own is the clearest indication that his own narrative lacks both," he said, adding: "Such attacks are contemptible, but their danger is decided by who will listen and who will challenge such bigotry." Hagee argued that describing Jesus as Palestinian because Bethlehem is today in the Palestinian-controlled West Bank would be anachronistic, comparing it to calling television personality Dr. Phil Cherokee simply because he was born in Oklahoma. "History also disproves what the ambassador is saying. The Romans intentionally adopted the name ‘Palestine’ as a replacement for ‘Judea’ in an effort to erase the Jews from the land, roughly a century after Christ was crucified," he added. CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND Hagee, whose group counts over 10 million members, added, "no reasonable person should entertain its existence in the future — given the horrors of October 7 and the ongoing effort by radical Islamists to annihilate the Jewish people." Zomlot made the comments on Sept. 3 during a conversation with Humza Yousaf, the former first minister of Scotland, at the University of Bradford. He recalled that, during a private audience with the late Queen Elizabeth II arranged by the British Foreign Office, he told her, "Jesus is our gift to you." "The Bible is a Palestinian book, and it has been used against us. It has been rewritten to be used against the people of the Book," Zomlot continued. "We are the original Christians, all the names that you see here, all the saints that you hear about came from my land and I am so proud about that, spreading Jesus’ message worldwide." Critics contend the Palestinian Authority has sought to shape the international historical narrative surrounding the land through institutions such as UNESCO and the United Nations. They point to UNESCO’s designation of the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron in the name of the "State of Palestine" in 2016 and its 2023 designation of Tell es-Sultan near Jericho as a World Heritage site in "Palestine." General Assembly resolution that referred to the Temple Mount, Judaism’s holiest site, only by its Muslim name, "Haram al-Sharif," as well as P.A. chief Mahmoud Abbas’ 2024 assertion that the site is the "exclusive property of Muslims." Critics also point to efforts to use Arabic names for sites with longstanding Jewish associations, such as Rachel’s Tomb in Nablus (Shechem), which is referred to as the "Bilal Bin Rabah Mosque." Ze’ev Orenstein, director of international affairs for the City of David Foundation in Jerusalem, told Fox News Digital that the origins of Islam date to the time of the Prophet Muhammad, about 1,300 years ago, while Jesus lived about 2,000 years ago and King David about 3,000 years ago. Orenstein noted that Jesus himself was Jewish, as were his disciples, and that he knew the Hebrew Bible, observed the Sabbath and Jewish dietary laws and celebrated Jewish festivals including Passover. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "To somehow say that Jesus was a Palestinian or that the Bible comes from 'Palestine,' no. Jesus lived in a place called Judea, and Jews come from Judea," he said. Orenstein said Zomlot was attempting to appropriate the religious and historical identity of Jews and Christians by attributing the foundations of their faith to a country he said did not exist in that form at the time. articles.body: As midterm races gear up for the November elections, the "Ruthless Podcast" discussed the latest financial allegations against prominent Democratic candidates in two marquee contests that the hosts said the mainstream media have neglected to cover. "It's just a couple of stories about states that you might not live or vote in, but you need to understand the kind of people Democrats are putting forward to represent their party," podcast co-host John Ashbrook said of two stories. Ashbrook's comments followed reporting from the Washington Free Beacon that Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine, co-sponsored a 2024 bill that called for $13.4 million in additional funding for Maine Maritime Academy while his son, Chace Jackson, served as the school's legislative designee. Jackson had also backed a 2023 state budget that provided the academy with an additional $2 million per year. "[These stories] are indicative of this larger thing that we've talked about, which is Democrats get into government so they can steer funds to their preferred parties," podcast co-host Josh Holmes said. "Sometimes they benefit directly, as they do here, and sometimes they have preferential constituencies that they then pay to vote for them to stay in office, like Minnesota." PLATNER'S REPLACEMENT FACES NEW SENATE CAMPAIGN HEADACHE TIED TO HIS SON'S LOBBYING Jackson will face Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a high-profile U.S. Senate race. Adam Gray, D-Calif., helped advance gas tax legislation that directed funds to his cousin’s newly established construction company. "This guy's like, no, no. Just give me $500,000." Gray faces former Stockton Mayor Kevin Lincoln II in the general election.
